Resurrection Plants

By: Diana Lucas | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Proffessor and the Plant

Summary:
Growing up on a farm in the Limpopo valley, Jill Farrant remembers as a nine year old, playing in an area they called Flat Rocks- a dead and dry river bed. But after rain that night it was alive and green with moss. What she didn’t know then was this plant was called M. flabellifolia, a moss with remarkable properties, one of which was to revitalize within 12 hours of a tiny amount of rain.

“I still have the little paper diary that I wrote it in……I told my dad but he wouldn’t believe me but it stayed with me and many years later after my PHD I went back to the farm and started collecting plants that are now called resurrection plants and they have become the basis of my life’s work ever since.”

Prof Jill Farrant is a molecular and cell biologist at the University of Cape Town. Her drive to isolate the gene sequence of plants she calls Resurrection Plants has earned her international recognition, awards and she’s featured in major documentaries.


Further information:
Her first case study, M. flabellifolia all those years ago led her to discover 135 species in the world of this very rare breed of plants, called resurrection plants because they appear to resurrect from the dead. These plants can lose up to 95% of their water and appear completely dead but bloom back to life in as little as 12 hours after rain.

“…they are not dead at all, they are just so dry that they look dead but you just have to add water.”

For Jill this has major implications in the world we live in today and our children will live in tomorrow.

“Climate change is one of the biggest environmental threats that we are going to be facing in the next 20 years and of course the consequences of that is always going to be on our food security.”

Because 95 % of world plant food supplies are predominantly maize, wheat or rice, that rely on annual rainfall, climate change models predict extreme weather conditions. That formerly predicable annual rainfall is not going to happen, while the volume of rain is likely going to be too much, leading to flooding, or too little, leading to drought. Both are devastating for grain production and hence food security.

In Africa where most of agriculture is rain fed this is a crisis. Very little on this planet tolerates water loss. All organisms are comprised predominately of water and loss of a small amount of that results in death. Resurrection plants are astounding: they can lose 95% of their water and remain in that dry state for months or even years and revive in 12 to 38 hours when water is supplied.

“What I am trying to do as a molecular physiologist is understand, how can they lose all that water and not die? And to use those mechanisms to make drought-tolerant crops that will go a long way to provide food security for Africa in the future.”

The majority of land plants provide seeds that are dry and are desiccation tolerant. Because Jill had a very early conviction that seeds and resurrection plants are switching on the same genes she and her team at UCT did experiments to prove that. Sequencing a genome of a resurrection plant was their final confirmation that they are using the core set of genes (like seeds) in order to withstand water deprivation.
Farrant is trying to identify and replicate the genes that help these “resurrection plants” defy death. She and her team at UCT’s research unit have contributed to the understanding of mechanisms used by resurrection plants to tolerate desiccation. This knowledge has been fundamental to identifying characteristics (genes) that might be important for use in bioengineering crops for improved drought tolerance.
“So we are trying to work out what the environmental and cellular signals are that turn on these genes in resurrection plants. Everything from water content, light, sugar, electrical signals, volatile signals. What switches that gene on and once we have understood that, we would like to use bio technology to activate existing genes that are in crops so that they are able to respond to environmental and cellular signals that are in drought by turning on mechanisms to tolerate water loss. I really do believe that my dream of making drought tolerant crops is possible. For a subsistence farmer in Africa this could be ground-breaking.”

Today a high proportion of papers published about resurrection plants are from Farrant’s laboratory, an under-resourced facility compared to her colleagues in Europe.

“But I am lucky. Of the 134 resurrection plants that exist, only three or four grow in Europe. The rest are in Africa.”

Jill’s research has brought international recognition, the UNESCO Award for Women in Science; fellow of the World Academy of Sciences; lectures at the prestigious Falling Walls Conference in Berlin; the Harry Oppenheimer Fellowship Award. Her work featured in several documentaries including the BBC’s ‘Genius Behind’ and ‘Food Parcels’.

And then late last year another somewhat different arrow was added to her quiver. Giorgio Armani sought Jill out to work with him on a new skin care range. The star of this show being her very first case study the moss Myrothamnus flabellifolia

“The secret of this plant is it contains a very powerful antioxidant and a simple sugar which stimulates the plant’s immune system, allowing it to break down toxins and turn that into vital energy for plant survival. The reality is that humans can benefit from the properties of this plant…particularly the skin.”

M. flabellifolia is believed to be one of the most ancient plants on the planet. Its name in indigenous languages roughly translates as ‘awake from the dead’. It’s widely used in African traditional medicine. This moss contains the greatest number of anti-oxidants Farrant has ever seen in a plant, more than so-called wonder plants rooibos and aloe vera. The major antioxidant in M. flabellifolia protects cell membranes from damage at the microscopic level – more effectively than vitamin C.
Giorgio Armani is using it as the main ingredient in his anti-aging cream, Crema Nera and with Jill on the scientific advisory board the future of this plant with its valuable properties is protected. Whilst M. flabellifolio can be grown en-masse in green houses, studies have shown this changes the composition of the plant – in other words when it does not need to produce strong anti-oxidants to survive it doesn’t. And as interest in this plant grows, so too does the risk of extinction if harvested un-checked. So Jill is working to ensure steps are taken to protect this valuable botanical source and remunerate the communities living with it.
Presently South Africa does not export the plant, it’s sourced from Zimbabwe. As a condition of her role as scientific advisor the plants will only be sourced from South Africa when there is investment into studies for sustainable harvesting. Despite not having industry funding Jill has already initiated studies to investigate the growth and reproductive rate of M. flabellifolia which will show the way to sustainable harvesting practices.
Jill is also working to ensure the farmers and communities who will grow the plant benefit and that royalties are paid to the elders of the communities who first discovered its medicinal properties.
Cosmetics companies other than Armani are also very interested in M. flabellifolia, and for Jill these conditions for her potential co-operation will remain in place for all of them.
With purpose, Prof Jill is today more committed to her research and students than ever before, and arguably one of the most progressive women in the scientific world today.
She considers herself lucky in her career and is committed to paying that forward to underprivileged students in her lab. As part of this effort, she uses much of the income she gets from Armani and other sources to top-up the income and subsidies of her students and level the playing field as much as possible.
“It is in my nature to support the underdog be they plant or human. And there is no more satisfying feeling than watching that little underdog rise to the top and become a real player in the field.”
A powerfully proudly South African story that brings the very urgent issue of climate change into the picture in a very personal way. And visually rich, with video and photos of Jill’s early life on the farm, with her students in the lab and in field research, the experiments in her lab and using extreme close ups fast forwards of her plants coming back to life and of desert areas blooming.

Script:


DEREK; Myrohthamnus Flabellifolia
Jill; We call it Myro..

Jill: Myro very special to me I have a little campaign going called Save the Myro and that’s basically to save this plant for our use in the future

V/O
To understand why its future preservation may be crucial to dealing with our coming challenges, we first need a trip into the past.”

Link
Molecular biologist Prof Jill Farrant has had a long love affair with Myro. They first met on a farm in the Waterberg, Limpopo when she was just 9 years old.

V/O
Jill remembers playing in an area on their farm called “flat rocks” – a dead and dry river bed.

Prof Jill Farrant
Department of Molecular and Cell Biology
University of Cape Town

Jill; I noticed the phenomenon of what we call R P dead looking plants coming alive after rain and I did mention this to my father, he didn’t really take me seriously.

V/O
The plant 9 year-old Jill had seen wondrously reviving was what she now calls Myro.

Link
What Jill didn’t know then was that Myro would play a significant part in her life and bring her research to world attention.

V/O
But it was 20 years before Jill – after completing her PHD and post doc - went back to the farm to collect samples of the plants she had noticed as a child. This was the beginning of her investigation into the phenomenon of Resurrection Plants. The basis of her life’s work.

Derek; What is so special about Resurrection Plants?
Jill; They are the only plants in the world that can lose all their water and not die. Most plants can lose between 10 and 20% of their water nothing can survive as much as 95% loss so it’s a very rare phenomenon.

Derek; How long does it take for these plants to revive?
Jill; Depends on the species, most of them take 12 hours to be totally green and fully hydrated.

V/O
To witness this for ourselves, we picked a few rather dead-looking sprigs of this resurrection plant…. that grows wild in the Cape.

Jill; so this little fern on table mountain if you look really closely it’s got orange hairs, and those hairs sense relative humidity and water and in fact allow leaf to open up, and it’s absolutely exquisite and a can’t wait to show you how it resurrects.

Derek: And we’re going to put it to the test tomorrow.

V/O
The next morning, in Jill’s lab at the University of Cape Town, we set up cameras, added water and waited.

Within 10 minutes the leaves started moving, unfurling. After an hour and 17 minutes they were noticeably greener and alive.

Jill; I was a farmer’s daughter. One is always very aware of the weather, particularly rain

V/O
Or as is often the case here, a lack of rain. A plant apparently dead one minute, green, and alive the next got this farmer’s daughter thinking

……and so to understand the phenomena of a plant that can lose all its water and not die immediately made me think - beautiful crops because I mean how many days would you cry for rain, and everything died. I can reverse that though this research . I am trying to make crops that can lose all their water but not die.

V/O
With climate change and extreme weather conditions a reality, nature is offering us a means of survival … plants that refuse to die could lead to a breakthrough in food security.

And that’s about more than simply helping drought-stricken farmers.  It’s about finding ways of helping humanity through what many are calling a coming catastrophe.”

Jill: The predictions are that by 2050 SA is going to be a desert with not enough rain to sustain any agriculture and if we can in fact have Resurrection crops at least we know we’re gonna get food.

V/O
As a molecular physiologist Jill is trying to understand how these plants lose all their water and stay alive.

Jill; We came to the understanding what they are actually using are seed genes now you and I know we can go and buy a packet of seeds they are dried out leave them in cupboards weeks or months and they are still alive so they are desiccated but alive. RP are desiccated but alive and they have used their seed genes in their roots and leaves.

V/O
So it’s the seeds that effectively contain the instruction booklet, the genes to switch the plant back to life. By identifying and isolating the gene sequence that holds this property, they can re programme other crops; like maize. to take on the ability to resurrect, to come back to life

Link
The big mission for Jill and her students at the UCT research unit is to identify and replicate these genes in RP which actually help them to defy death.

Shandry Tebele
Department of Molecular and Cell Biology
University of Cape Town

V/O
PHD student Shandry Tebele……has a personal motive in her research.

Shandry; The reason I started this research is because my grandmother, she was a farmer and so she would struggle during farming, find that there is no water, because I am from Limpopo and Limpopo is very dry and it’s hot. So for me to tap into this research is to find solutions. OK, if I get these these special microbes we can use them and assist a lot of farmers to overcome the drought problem in the world and South Africa.

Derek: And you could be helping your family in Limpopo

Shandry: Yes, back home

Link
240 of these resurrection plants that virtually awaken from the dead have been identified around the world and all but a handful are from Africa.

Jill; in fact Myro is one of the most well known Resurrection plants because it’s so distinct. It sits on the rock it looks like hell and it rains the next day…, you know, it’s bright and green, very very distinctive

V/O
Myro and the other ancient resurrection plants have been used in traditional African medicine for centuries.

Jill: For many years one of the nicknames for Myro is Bobbejaan dagga because if you smoke the dry leaves it’s a anti asthmatic, you don’t get a high.

V/O
For Jill and her students, the mountain is their playground – bursting with biological and botanical diversity.

Up sound: Derek: That is stunning. It’s like you’re painting with green.

V/O Credit courtesy @Fondation L’Oréal.

It’s a passion that has brought Jill huge acclaim, winning her numerous awards and nominations. And then, she discovered her favourite plant, Myro, had properties that led her into a whole new world.

MINUS 15 SEC
Link
Italian designer Giorgio Armani was interested in the characteristics of this plant and how it could possibly be used in cosmetics.

Credit courtesy @Fondation L’Oréal.

Jill; Gorgio Armani decided to make Myrothamnus active in a skin care range which he has called Crema Nera Extrema. so I was invited to be the scientific consultant.

Derek: So Jill if I look at my gnarly hands bit of Myro might help there in a cream?

Jill: Myro could definitely help in that cream you have a very rich anti oxidant protection.

Derek: Higher than Vitamin C?

Jill: Much higher, 30 times higher, I mean this is a powerful anti oxidant. It really is. The plant also makes certain sugars... So this little sugar stimulates your skin breaking down all the toxins and regenerating good stuff for continued cell division and growth.

Credit courtesy @Fondation L’Oréal.

Derek: You were interviewed by Cate Blanchett

Jill: Yes I was. I spent the whole weekend in the villa being interviewed and talked about couple of seconds about me all about Cate.

Derek: Been part of your life science you were 9 years old.
Jill: Ya I kind of think sometimes destiny thing I was meant to do this.

Derek: And we’re going to put it to the test tomorrow. V/O The next morning, in Jill’s lab at the University of Cape Town, we set up cameras, added water and waited. Within 10 minutes the leaves started moving, unfurling. After an hour and 17 minutes they were noticeably greener and alive. Jill; I was a farmer’s daughter. One is always very aware of the weather, particularly rain V/O Or as is often the case here, a lack of rain. A plant apparently dead one minute, green, and alive the next got this farmer’s daughter thinking ……and so to understand the phenomena of a plant that can lose all its water and not die immediately made me think - beautiful crops because I mean how many days would you cry for rain, and everything died. I can reverse that though this research . I am trying to make crops that can lose all their water but not die. V/O With climate change and extreme weather conditions a reality, nature is offering us a means of survival … plants that refuse to die could lead to a breakthrough in food security. And that’s about more than simply helping drought-stricken farmers. It’s about finding ways of helping humanity through what many are calling a coming catastrophe.” Jill: The predictions are that by 2050 SA is going to be a desert with not enough rain to sustain any agriculture and if we can in fact have Resurrection crops at least we know we’re gonna get food. V/O As a molecular physiologist Jill is trying to understand how these plants lose all their water and stay alive. Jill; We came to the understanding what they are actually using are seed genes now you and I know we can go and buy a packet of seeds they are dried out leave them in cupboards weeks or months and they are still alive so they are desiccated but alive. RP are desiccated but alive and they have used their seed genes in their roots and leaves. V/O So it’s the seeds that effectively contain the instruction booklet, the genes to switch the plant back to life. By identifying and isolating the gene sequence that holds this property, they can re programme other crops; like maize. to take on the ability to resurrect, to come back to life Link The big mission for Jill and her students at the UCT research unit is to identify and replicate these genes in RP which actually help them to defy death. Shandry Tebele Department of Molecular and Cell Biology University of Cape Town V/O PHD student Shandry Tebele……has a personal motive in her research. Shandry; The reason I started this research is because my grandmother, she was a farmer and so she would struggle during farming, find that there is no water, because I am from Limpopo and Limpopo is very dry and it’s hot. So for me to tap into this research is to find solutions. OK, if I get these these special microbes we can use them and assist a lot of farmers to overcome the drought problem in the world and South Africa. Derek: And you could be helping your family in Limpopo Shandry: Yes, back home Link 240 of these resurrection plants that virtually awaken from the dead have been identified around the world and all but a handful are from Africa. Jill; in fact Myro is one of the most well known Resurrection plants because it’s so distinct. It sits on the rock it looks like hell and it rains the next day…, you know, it’s bright and green, very very distinctive V/O Myro and the other ancient resurrection plants have been used in traditional African medicine for centuries. Jill: For many years one of the nicknames for Myro is Bobbejaan dagga because if you smoke the dry leaves it’s a anti asthmatic, you don’t get a high. V/O For Jill and her students, the mountain is their playground – bursting with biological and botanical diversity. Up sound: Derek: That is stunning. It’s like you’re painting with green. V/O Credit courtesy @Fondation L’Oréal. It’s a passion that has brought Jill huge acclaim, winning her numerous awards and nominations. And then, she discovered her favourite plant, Myro, had properties that led her into a whole new world. MINUS 15 SEC Link Italian designer Giorgio Armani was interested in the characteristics of this plant and how it could possibly be used in cosmetics. Credit courtesy @Fondation L’Oréal. Jill; Gorgio Armani decided to make Myrothamnus active in a skin care range which he has called Crema Nera Extrema. so I was invited to be the scientific consultant. Derek: So Jill if I look at my gnarly hands bit of Myro might help there in a cream? Jill: Myro could definitely help in that cream you have a very rich anti oxidant protection. Derek: Higher than Vitamin C? Jill: Much higher, 30 times higher, I mean this is a powerful anti oxidant. It really is. The plant also makes certain sugars... So this little sugar stimulates your skin breaking down all the toxins and regenerating good stuff for continued cell division and growth. Credit courtesy @Fondation L’Oréal. Derek: You were interviewed by Cate Blanchett Jill: Yes I was. I spent the whole weekend in the villa being interviewed and talked about couple of seconds about me all about Cate. Derek: Been part of your life science you were 9 years old. Jill: Ya I kind of think sometimes destiny thing I was meant to do this.

metadata.Summary: Growing up on a farm in the Limpopo valley, Jill Farrant remembers as a nine year old, playing in an area they called Flat Rocks- a dead and dry river bed. But after rain that night it was alive and green with moss. What she didn’t know then was this plant was called M. flabellifolia, a moss with remarkable properties, one of which was to revitalize within 12 hours of a tiny amount of rain. “I still have the little paper diary that I wrote it in……I told my dad but he wouldn’t believe me but it stayed with me and many years later after my PHD I went back to the farm and started collecting plants that are now called resurrection plants and they have become the basis of my life’s work ever since.” Prof Jill Farrant is a molecular and cell biologist at the University of Cape Town. Her drive to isolate the gene sequence of plants she calls Resurrection Plants has earned her international recognition, awards and she’s featured in major documentaries.
metadata.Further information: Her first case study, M. flabellifolia all those years ago led her to discover 135 species in the world of this very rare breed of plants, called resurrection plants because they appear to resurrect from the dead. These plants can lose up to 95% of their water and appear completely dead but bloom back to life in as little as 12 hours after rain. “…they are not dead at all, they are just so dry that they look dead but you just have to add water.” For Jill this has major implications in the world we live in today and our children will live in tomorrow. “Climate change is one of the biggest environmental threats that we are going to be facing in the next 20 years and of course the consequences of that is always going to be on our food security.” Because 95 % of world plant food supplies are predominantly maize, wheat or rice, that rely on annual rainfall, climate change models predict extreme weather conditions. That formerly predicable annual rainfall is not going to happen, while the volume of rain is likely going to be too much, leading to flooding, or too little, leading to drought. Both are devastating for grain production and hence food security. In Africa where most of agriculture is rain fed this is a crisis. Very little on this planet tolerates water loss. All organisms are comprised predominately of water and loss of a small amount of that results in death. Resurrection plants are astounding: they can lose 95% of their water and remain in that dry state for months or even years and revive in 12 to 38 hours when water is supplied. “What I am trying to do as a molecular physiologist is understand, how can they lose all that water and not die? And to use those mechanisms to make drought-tolerant crops that will go a long way to provide food security for Africa in the future.” The majority of land plants provide seeds that are dry and are desiccation tolerant. Because Jill had a very early conviction that seeds and resurrection plants are switching on the same genes she and her team at UCT did experiments to prove that. Sequencing a genome of a resurrection plant was their final confirmation that they are using the core set of genes (like seeds) in order to withstand water deprivation. Farrant is trying to identify and replicate the genes that help these “resurrection plants” defy death. She and her team at UCT’s research unit have contributed to the understanding of mechanisms used by resurrection plants to tolerate desiccation. This knowledge has been fundamental to identifying characteristics (genes) that might be important for use in bioengineering crops for improved drought tolerance. “So we are trying to work out what the environmental and cellular signals are that turn on these genes in resurrection plants. Everything from water content, light, sugar, electrical signals, volatile signals. What switches that gene on and once we have understood that, we would like to use bio technology to activate existing genes that are in crops so that they are able to respond to environmental and cellular signals that are in drought by turning on mechanisms to tolerate water loss. I really do believe that my dream of making drought tolerant crops is possible. For a subsistence farmer in Africa this could be ground-breaking.” Today a high proportion of papers published about resurrection plants are from Farrant’s laboratory, an under-resourced facility compared to her colleagues in Europe. “But I am lucky. Of the 134 resurrection plants that exist, only three or four grow in Europe. The rest are in Africa.” Jill’s research has brought international recognition, the UNESCO Award for Women in Science; fellow of the World Academy of Sciences; lectures at the prestigious Falling Walls Conference in Berlin; the Harry Oppenheimer Fellowship Award. Her work featured in several documentaries including the BBC’s ‘Genius Behind’ and ‘Food Parcels’. And then late last year another somewhat different arrow was added to her quiver. Giorgio Armani sought Jill out to work with him on a new skin care range. The star of this show being her very first case study the moss Myrothamnus flabellifolia “The secret of this plant is it contains a very powerful antioxidant and a simple sugar which stimulates the plant’s immune system, allowing it to break down toxins and turn that into vital energy for plant survival. The reality is that humans can benefit from the properties of this plant…particularly the skin.” M. flabellifolia is believed to be one of the most ancient plants on the planet. Its name in indigenous languages roughly translates as ‘awake from the dead’. It’s widely used in African traditional medicine. This moss contains the greatest number of anti-oxidants Farrant has ever seen in a plant, more than so-called wonder plants rooibos and aloe vera. The major antioxidant in M. flabellifolia protects cell membranes from damage at the microscopic level – more effectively than vitamin C. Giorgio Armani is using it as the main ingredient in his anti-aging cream, Crema Nera and with Jill on the scientific advisory board the future of this plant with its valuable properties is protected. Whilst M. flabellifolio can be grown en-masse in green houses, studies have shown this changes the composition of the plant – in other words when it does not need to produce strong anti-oxidants to survive it doesn’t. And as interest in this plant grows, so too does the risk of extinction if harvested un-checked. So Jill is working to ensure steps are taken to protect this valuable botanical source and remunerate the communities living with it. Presently South Africa does not export the plant, it’s sourced from Zimbabwe. As a condition of her role as scientific advisor the plants will only be sourced from South Africa when there is investment into studies for sustainable harvesting. Despite not having industry funding Jill has already initiated studies to investigate the growth and reproductive rate of M. flabellifolia which will show the way to sustainable harvesting practices. Jill is also working to ensure the farmers and communities who will grow the plant benefit and that royalties are paid to the elders of the communities who first discovered its medicinal properties. Cosmetics companies other than Armani are also very interested in M. flabellifolia, and for Jill these conditions for her potential co-operation will remain in place for all of them. With purpose, Prof Jill is today more committed to her research and students than ever before, and arguably one of the most progressive women in the scientific world today. She considers herself lucky in her career and is committed to paying that forward to underprivileged students in her lab. As part of this effort, she uses much of the income she gets from Armani and other sources to top-up the income and subsidies of her students and level the playing field as much as possible. “It is in my nature to support the underdog be they plant or human. And there is no more satisfying feeling than watching that little underdog rise to the top and become a real player in the field.” A powerfully proudly South African story that brings the very urgent issue of climate change into the picture in a very personal way. And visually rich, with video and photos of Jill’s early life on the farm, with her students in the lab and in field research, the experiments in her lab and using extreme close ups fast forwards of her plants coming back to life and of desert areas blooming.
